evidence_notes: Claim: limiting car use makes life less hectic and cleaner (source-based, cites Sources 1-3). Support: Vauban Germany survey (70%/57%), Heidrun Walter quote; Paris driving ban and smog, 67% diesel; then a general public-transit alternative. org 4 (thesis early and held, frame present, but the 'less hectic' and 'cleaner' body parts swap freely - a set of supports, not a sequence); dev 4 (specific quoted support and connections stated - 'the use of these harsh fossil fuels is a huge problem that can help be controlled by limiting our use of automobiles' - but the third support is hypothetical/general so not specific throughout, and quotations sit alongside rather than inside the writer's sentences); conv 3 (spelling errors accumulate - servey, precent, incerance, feuls, convenent - and the France/diesel sentence and the unclosed long quote force re-reading to repair, though nothing has to be guessed); arg 4 (one reason genuinely reasoned - no car payments/insurance/gas is why the car-free life is less stressful - and the 'some may argue we need cars' objection is answered with alternatives, but the conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing implies, so rung 5's (d) fails)

Claim: becoming a Seagoing Cowboy is worth doing, for three previewed reasons (help people, see places, variety of activities). Support: Europe, China, Venice, Panama Canal; aunt Katie's farm, night watchman duty, list of games. org 4 (three previewed reasons stated early and held with a frame, but the three body parts are fully interchangeable); dev 4 (specific realized detail in parts 2 and 3, and the connection is stated at least once - 'gives you the once in a life time opportunity to see and go places where you might never get to go again' - but part 1 is general throughout and the activities are listed, so not specific-and-explained throughout); conv 3 (errors accumulate - varity, Bsaedall, In summery, 'be an Seagoing Cowboy' - and dropped subjects such as 'When you get there can be assigned a person' and 'on my to China' need repair on re-reading, nothing needs guessing); arg 4 (at least one reason reasoned - the once-in-a-lifetime warrant for why travel counts, and 'they fought for your country' as a warrant for helping - but no opposing view, no qualification, and the conclusion restates what the prompt implies)

Claim: the Face on Mars is not an alien artifact but a natural Martian mesa. Support drawn from the source: April 5 1998 Mars Global Surveyor photo ten times sharper than Viking 1; the haze objection answered by the cloudless April 8 2001 image; 1.56 m/pixel vs 43 m/pixel. org 4 (controlling idea first and held, frame present, and the 1998-then-2001 sequence is genuinely dependent, but the closing unit starts on what the landform is and finishes on an unsupported 'chance for NASA to get a little money', so band 5's unified idea-units and working closing both fail); dev 3 (capped by patchwriting - the pixel comparison, 'absolute maximum resolution' and 'Martian equivalent of a butte or mesa' are source phrasing lightly stitched with little transformation - and the figures are reported without saying what they show); conv 3 (errors accumulate - thoe, creat, tooken, revield, satisfi, clody - and the subjectless 'is just a natural land form' and 'when they finally found it Malins team' force re-reading, nothing needs guessing); arg 4 (one reason genuinely reasoned - shadows create the illusion of eyes, nose and mouth, which is why it looks like a face while being natural - and the haze objection is answered, but the conclusion is the one the prompt's framing already implies)

Claim: Luke should join the program because 'he might learn something new' / 'it might actually help him'. Support: no particulars from the article - only that Luke likes the Seagoing Cowboys and wants to be one; the last part leaves Luke entirely for the writer's own post-graduation plans. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated in the essay's own words in sentence one, but it is not held - there is no closing, the third part shifts to 'it's Luke's life, his choice' and the fourth to the writer's own future, and units carry several jobs at once); dev 2 (support is general throughout with no named case or particular from the article, and what is offered restates the claim - 'he wants to be a Seagoing Cowboy he wants to be a good person thats all he wants in his life'); conv 2 (meaning is somewhat obscured - 'Luke it all like well i kind a mightlike this program' and 'i eant ti ne a good person, intelligent a awsome person' have to be guessed at rather than repaired, on top of unpunctuated run-ons throughout); arg 2 (the position is the prompt's wording handed back with no commitment added, hedged with 'might' at every turn, and the reasons are restatements of the position in other words)

Claim: the Face on Mars was not made by aliens, announced as a thesis ('In this paper im going to prove to you...'). Support: the 25-years-ago discovery and return photographs, the first image caught in winter on a cloudy day, cameras that would capture 'the smallest of sheds' (cited as (11)), and the rock still being there. org 4 (thesis early and held, frame present, all parts on topic, and there is a real objection-then-answer pairing, but unmarked voice shifts - addressing NASA in one part and speaking as NASA in the next - plus closing units carrying several unrelated jobs keep band 5's unified idea-units out of reach); dev 4 (connections are stated - no life because a camera that resolves a shed would have shown a house; aliens destroyed nothing because the rock is still there - but the winter/cloudy detail is dropped without explanation and other support is vague, so not specific-and-explained throughout); conv 3 (errors accumulate - aleins, inteligent creaters, travled, takin, easely, plante, theroy - and broken word order plus the mid-clause break at 'On camera so if we saw a little house' force repair on re-reading, nothing needs guessing); arg 4 (reasoning is genuinely shown at least once via the camera-resolution inference, and the alien objection is both voiced and answered, but the conclusion goes no further than the prompt's framing already implies)

Claim: 'The face is just a natrual landform.' Nearly everything after that opening sentence is reproduced source text - the Viking 1 sister-ship narrative, the 'huge rock formation... which resembles a human head' caption, the pop-icon and conspiracy-theorist passage, the Sept 1997 / April 5 1998 Malin paragraph, 'Thousands of anxious web surfers were waiting... revealing... a natural landform', and the Garvin Middle Butte quotation. The writer's own words amount to the opening sentence, 'In the article it says that', and the closing sentence. org 4 (the position opens and holds, the source-derived chronology is dependent rather than interchangeable, but the opening is a bare thesis with no orientation, the closing only restates it, and units drift - the caption's authors' motive, the garbled 'defenders of the NASSA budget' clause); dev 1 (the response is predominantly copied - band 1(d) - so the borrowed material stands in for development entirely); conv 3 (judging the writer's own sentences plus transcription damage: notedd, aunthors, NASSA, sientists, Red Plant, Iidaho, heeight, and 'you can include' for 'conclude'; 'defenders of the NASSA budget with there was' and the mid-sentence paragraph break force re-reading, though meaning stays recoverable); arg 3 (the position is clear and held but never reasoned in the writer's own terms - the article's narrative is laid out and the conclusion asserted, and the closing circles back to the opening sentence in different words)

Claim: the Face is 'simply just a peculiar looking landform', with the essay announcing that counter-arguments must be answered. Support: theories traceable to books/magazines/movies sold for profit (general), then the 1976 photograph as the believers' sole basis, the 1998 photograph 'ten times sharper than the original Viking photos', and the camera-malfunction counter-argument dissolved by that same fact. org 6 (the sequence makes a nameable move - weakest to strongest, explicitly hinged at 'one must not forget the people who claim they have the scientifically correct reasoning' and 'a little more credible than the others' - the opening states what is at stake and what the essay will do, the closing lands a principle the opening did not, and every unit does one job); dev 4 (the 1998-photo support is specific and genuinely interpreted, but the whole commercialization part is general with no named title and its profit-motive claim is unsupported, so support is not specific throughout); conv 4 (varied sentence lengths and shapes, apt phrasing such as 'with a key emphasis on the fiction part', errors visible but not accumulating; band 5 fails because 'in which there is one fact' and the agreement slip in 'have been swiftly and easily disproven, and has been further proven' do cost a re-read); arg 5 (reasons are reasoned - the sharper camera invalidates the assumption behind the malfunction objection - an opposing position is acknowledged and answered, and the diagnosis that the theories originate in commercial fiction is a conclusion the prompt's framing does not imply; short of 6 because the NASA-concealment claim it raises is the strongest objection and is dropped unanswered, and it never reframes or bounds its position)

Claim: for the development of driverless cars, but qualified in the opening - 'I don't think we should completely have no control... Drivers should still pay attention to the road as if they were normally driving.' Support: disabled people who cannot drive deserve a way around town; the car remains an option since a driver can take over; long trips where flying is too expensive. org 4 (position early and held with a frame, but the three reasons are fully interchangeable - a set of supports rather than a sequence); dev 4 (the long-distance case is a realized scenario and connections are stated for several supports - 'People can buy a driverless car but still take over if they want to or need too' - but nothing is named, numeric or specific throughout, and the fault objection is waved away unsupported); conv 4 (errors are visible but do not accumulate - lowercase i, 'need too', 'more easier', 'depicted' for determined - and sentences vary; band 5 fails because the unpunctuated long-distance sentence and the wrong-footing 'easily depicted' do cost a small repair); arg 4 (one reason genuinely reasoned - disabled people deserve mobility, flying is too expensive for long trips - and the position is qualified in the opening, but the fault objection is mentioned without being engaged and the closing reverts to the unqualified prompt-implied conclusion, so rung 5's (d) fails)

Claim: 'I don't think the driverless cars are all that safe just yet', stated in the second part after an opening that lists benefits (economy, pollution, gas). Support: sensors could fail while driving and leave you broken down; can a local garage repair it; the rest is a run of open questions about laws, top speed, sensor cost, navigation and fuel. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated in the essay's own words but is weakly located mid-essay, the opening lists benefits that do not sit under it, and there is no closing at all - the essay stops on a question); dev 2 (after discarding the driver-boredom question and the fuel/speed/law questions, which do not bear on safety, what remains is a generic hypothetical with no named case or particular anywhere, and the economy/pollution/gas claims go entirely unsupported); conv 3 (errors accumulate - Driveless, polution, can u, some were, your driving, borewd, there turn, kno - and 'How long will the car last be in driverless mode' needs repair on re-reading; sentences run to one short pattern but meaning stays recoverable without guessing); arg 3 (the position is the writer's own and committed, but no reason is actually reasoned - the sensor worry is raised as a what-if and the essay never says why any of it makes the cars unsafe, and the final part retreats into questions rather than argument)

Claim: America should get rid of the electoral college and switch to popular vote. Support: the source's account that a vote is really for a state elector who then votes for the president; candidates skip states they cannot win; the phrase 'unfair, outdated, and irrational' repeated three times. org 3 (position stated early, but the third part repeats the second without adding to it, there are two redundant closings, and the position drifts at 'lets let them decide if we should keep it the same... or change it'); dev 3 (one specific piece of support - the elector mechanism - but it is source phrasing lightly stitched with 'unfair, outdated, and irrational' lifted whole, the winner-take-all point is listed with no explanation, and 'we should change it to popular vote because the electoral college is really unfair' is circular); conv 2 (meaning is somewhat obscured - 'you are in favor' and 'after all its what we choose then thats what we ned to be happening' have to be guessed at rather than repaired - on top of frequent errors including presedent/precedent, thier, Alote, elecoral, somthing, and fragments and run-ons throughout); arg 3 (the position is clear and committed but reasoning is asserted rather than shown - the mechanism is described and simply labelled unfair - and the last two parts restate the opening in different words, explicitly so at 'Like I said it is unfair, outdated, and irrational')
